Recap: while Mr. Rochester was away, his guests at Thornfield were visited by a gipsy fortune-teller who would see only the young, single ladies, one at a time, in the library. Blanche Ingram came back sullen; three other girls came back half-scared, saying she knew all about them. Now Jane, the governess, who loves Rochester and expects him to marry Blanche, has been sent for. Grace Poole is the servant Jane believes set fire to Rochester’s bed one night. “Nichered” means sniggered; to cross a palm with silver is to pay a fortune-teller; diablerie is devilry; “blackaviced” means dark-faced; a rent-roll is the income from an estate; “dished” means done for.
readings.contentNote: The fortune-teller is presented through period stereotypes of a Romani (“gipsy”) woman: dark-faced, pipe-smoking, telling fortunes for silver.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, from the opening through the gipsy’s talk of Miss Ingram and the Rochester estate; opens “The library looked tranquil enough as I entered it, and the Sibyl—if Sibyl she were—was…”; closes “…suitor to look out: if another comes, with a longer or clearer rent-roll,—he’s dished—””.

questions.prompt: “Why don’t you tremble?” “I’m not cold.” How does Jane answer the gipsy’s first challenges, and how does the gipsy turn her answers around?
facilitatorNotes: Short, literal, unimpressed replies, after warning that she has “no faith.” The gipsy then turns Jane’s own words: cold because alone, sick because love keeps away, silly because she will not move toward it. It is reasoning about Jane’s life, not prophecy. Ask which of the three charges hits home.
evidence: I’m not silly.
You are cold, because you are alone

questions.prompt: Jane says this could be said of almost anyone in her position. How does the gipsy answer, and what is she hinting?
facilitatorNotes: The gipsy asks Jane to “find me another precisely placed as you are”: Jane is “very near happiness,” the materials ready, wanting only “a movement to combine them.” The riddle points at someone in the house who might return her feeling. Jane’s “I don’t understand enigmas” is a parry; she has every reason not to understand.
evidence: very near happiness; yes, within reach of it
I don’t understand enigmas.

questions.prompt: Why does the name “Mrs. Poole” bring Jane to her feet?
facilitatorNotes: Jane suspects Grace Poole of the fire in Rochester’s room and the strange laughter in the house; hearing the name from a stranger makes the gipsy seem to know secrets, “diablerie” after all. The gipsy calls Grace “a safe hand” and “close and quiet,” an odd recommendation. Readers can note that Jane’s fear is about Grace, not about the fortune-teller.
evidence: I started to my feet when I heard the name.
there is diablerie in the business after all, then!

questions.prompt: The gipsy presses Jane about Mr. Rochester and Miss Ingram. What does Jane refuse to say, and what does the gipsy give away by saying too much?
facilitatorNotes: Jane deflects (“He is not at home”), falls silent when asked what she “detected,” and says she came “to inquire, not to confess.” The gipsy knows Rochester’s habits, calls him a “blackaviced suitor,” says Blanche loves at least “his purse,” and admits telling her something that made her “wondrous grave.” Why would a wandering fortune-teller care so much? Readers may begin to suspect.
evidence: I came here to inquire, not to confess
if not his person, at least his purse

readings.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: the gipsy unmasked, and a name from the West Indies (Chapter XIX, end)
readings.challenge: Reread the reading of Jane’s face once you know who spoke it, and weigh Jane’s judgment of the trick.
readings.focus: Rochester’s disguise reveals more of him than of Jane, and one name turns him white.
readings.context: Recap: in the library the gipsy read Jane’s life back to her: alone, close to happiness if she would reach for it, and watching Rochester and Blanche Ingram, whom the gipsy says he will marry, though Blanche may love his purse more than him. Jane insisted she came for her own fortune. A guest arrived while Rochester was away: Mr. Mason, from Jamaica in the West Indies, who says he is an old friend. The “still small voice” after wind, earthquake and fire comes from the Bible (1 Kings 19); “Off, ye lendings!” is King Lear’s cry as he tears off his clothes; a ministrant spirit is a ministering angel.
readings.contentNote: Rochester has disguised himself as a “gipsy” woman, playing the period’s stereotype.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, from Jane’s “I came to hear my own” to the end of the chapter; opens ““But, mother, I did not come to hear Mr. Rochester’s fortune: I came to hear my own; and…”; closes “He spoke cheerfully: the gay tones set my heart at ease. I was soon asleep.”.

questions.prompt: The fortune-teller reads Jane’s eye, mouth and brow. What does the forehead “say,” and why is it the one “enemy to a fortunate issue”?
facilitatorNotes: “I can live alone, if self-respect, and circumstances require”; “I need not sell my soul to buy bliss”; reason holds the reins and conscience has the casting vote. Jane will not take happiness at a price she cannot afford, and that, the speaker sees, may stand in the way. Ask whether this is a fair portrait of the Jane readers know.
evidence: I need not sell my soul to buy bliss.
but judgment shall still have the last word in every argument

questions.prompt: Then the speaker says, “I have formed my plans—right plans I deem them.” Whose plans are these, and what nearly slips out before “That will do”?
facilitatorNotes: The voice is now Rochester’s own: he wants “to foster, not to blight,” his harvest “in smiles, in endearments, in sweet—” and he stops, calling it “exquisite delirium.” He has governed himself “thoroughly,” but “further might try me beyond my strength.” He has nearly declared himself. Readers can debate what “right plans” means for a man about to marry Blanche.
evidence: my harvest must be in smiles, in endearments, in sweet—That will do.
but further might try me beyond my strength

questions.prompt: Jane tells Rochester “it was not right.” What was he after, and had Jane been on her guard?
facilitatorNotes: He was “trying to draw me out—or in”: to learn her feelings while hiding his. Jane had suspected a masquerade from the feigned voice and hidden face, but her mind ran on Grace Poole: “I had never thought of Mr. Rochester.” She concludes she was “very correct,” and congratulates herself. Readers can weigh how unfair the trick was, from an employer to a governess.
evidence: you have been talking nonsense to make me talk nonsense
I had never thought of Mr. Rochester.

questions.prompt: “Mason!—the West Indies!” How does Rochester react, and what does he ask Jane? What do her answers show?
facilitatorNotes: He grips her wrist, turns “whiter than ashes,” repeats the words like an automaton, and wishes for “a quiet island with only you” away from “hideous recollections.” He asks whether she would stay if everyone shunned him. She would, but only for a friend “who deserved my adherence”: her loyalty is warm but conditional. The cheerful voice at bedtime eases her, and perhaps should not.
evidence: Jane, I’ve got a blow; I’ve got a blow, Jane!
I could dare it for the sake of any friend who deserved my adherence; as you, I am sure, do.
